e-6861.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Distinct Real Roots
e-6861.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
y'' + y - 2y =0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y = Ae^{x} + Be^{- 2 x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
y'' + y - 2y =0,
\ \ y(1) = e, \ \ y'(1) = e ^{-2}.
$$
e-6861.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=e$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}e & =A{e}^{1}+B{e}^{-2(1)} \\ e & =Ae+B{e}^{-2} \\ A & =1-B{e}^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition $y'(1) = e^{-2},$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
y' = Ae^x - 2Be^{-x}.
$$

Then, we substitute $y'(1)=e^{-2}$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2} & =A{e}^{1}-2B{e}^{-2(1)} \\ {e}^{-2} & =Ae-2B{e}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A=1-B{e}^{-3} \\ {e}^{-2}=Ae-2B{e}^{-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $A = 1 - B e ^{-3}$ in the second equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2} & =(1-B{e}^{-3})e-2B{e}^{-2} \\ 1 & ={e}^{3}-B-2B \\ B & =\frac{{e}^{3}-1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting $B= \dfrac {e ^ 3 - 1} 3$ back into the equation $A = 1-Be^{-3}$ gives

$$
A = 1 -  \dfrac {(e ^ 3 - 1) e ^ {-3}} 3 =   \dfrac {2 +  e ^ {-3}} 3.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution of the initial value problem is

$$
y =  \dfrac {  e ^ {-3} + 2} 3  e^{x} + \dfrac {e ^ 3 - 1} 3 e^{-2x}.
$$

e-6862.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Repeated Roots
e-6862.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
y'' - 4 y' + 4y =0,
\qquad y(0) =  3, \qquad y'(0) = 2.
$$
e-6862.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We have a repeated root $\lambda = 2,$ so we have the following general solution:

$$
y = A e ^ { 2 x} + B x e ^ {2 x}
$$

We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=3$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =A{e}^{2(0)}+B(0){e}^{2(0)} \\ 3 & =A{e}^{0}+0 \\ 3 & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition $y' (0) = 2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
y'  = 2 A e ^ {2 x} +  B e ^ { 2 x} + 2 B x e ^{ 2 x}.
$$

Then, we substitute $y'(0)=2$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2A{e}^{2(0)}+B{e}^{2(0)}+2B(0){e}^{2(0)} \\ 2 & =2A{e}^{0}+B{e}^{0}+0 \\ 2 & =2A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3=A \\ 2=2A+B\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $A=3$ into the second equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =6+B \\ B & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $A=3$ and $B=-4,$ and therefore the solution is 

$$
y = 3 e ^ { 2 x } - 4 x e ^ { 2 x}.
$$

e-6791.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Imaginary Roots
e-6791.problem:
Solve the following initial value problem:

$$
y'' + y = 0, \quad y(\pi) = 2, \quad y'(\pi) = -1
$$
e-6791.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
y = A \cos x + B \sin x
$$

Now, we need to find constants $A$ and $B.$ To do this, we apply the initial conditions $y(\pi)=2,$ $y'(\pi)=-1.$

- Substituting $y(\pi) = 2$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\pi ) & =2 \\ A\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +B\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi  & =2 \\ -A & =2 \\ A & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing $y'(x),$ we get

$$
y' =  - A \sin{x} + B\cos{x},
$$

and substituting $y'(\pi)=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\pi ) & =-1 \\ -A\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +B\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  & =-1 \\ -B & =-1 \\ B & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y = -2\cos{x} + \sin{x}.
$$

e-7051.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots
e-7051.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
y'' - 6y' + 25y=0, \quad y(0)= 2,  \quad y'(0) = 5, \quad t\gt 0.
$$
e-7051.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +25 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9)-9+25 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-3)^{2}+16 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda -3 & =4\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =3\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
y = e^{3x} \left( P \cos 4x + Q \sin 4x \right)
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0) = 2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2 = P.
$$

- To apply the condition $y'(0) = 5,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =3{e}^{3x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+{e}^{3x}(-4P\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+4Q\operatorname{cos}⁡4x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $y'(0) = 5$ and $P=2$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =3{e}^{0}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡0+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡0)+{e}^{0}(-4(2)\operatorname{sin}⁡0+4Q\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\ 5 & =6+4Q \\ -1 & =4Q \\ Q & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y = e^{3x} \left( 2 \cos 4x - \dfrac{1}{4} \sin 4x \right).
$$

Solve the initial value problem y″−5y′−14y=0,y(1)=2,  y′(1)=5.

y=e−2x+2+e7x−7
b
y=4e−3x−2e4x

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation r^2-5r-14=(r-7)(r+2)=0 gives y=Ae^{-2(x-1)}+Be^{7(x-1)}. The initial conditions imply A+B=2 and -2A+7B=5, so A=B=1. Thus option a satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-5\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}-14{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -14) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -14 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
(\lambda +2)(\lambda -7)=0,
$$

and so $\lambda =-2$ or $\lambda =7.$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{7x}.
$$

Now let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
A{e}^{-2}+B{e}^{7}=2.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=5.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-2A{e}^{-2x}+7B{e}^{7x}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the above gives

$$
-2A{e}^{-2}+7B{e}^{7}=5.
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A{e}^{-2}+B{e}^{7}=2 \\ -2A{e}^{-2}+7B{e}^{7}=5\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A={e}^{2},B={e}^{-7}.$

Now we get the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2}\cdot {e}^{-2x}+{e}^{-7}\cdot {e}^{7x} \\ y & ={e}^{-2x+2}+{e}^{7x-7}\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

Solve the initial value problem y″−5y′−14y=0,y(1)=2,  y′(1)=5.

a
y=e−2x+2+e7x−7
b
y=4e−3x−2e4x
c
y=5e−2x+2−3e7x−7
d
y=e3x−3+e4x−4
e
y=4e−2x+2−2e7x−7
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let y=eλx. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λeλx,y″=λ2eλx.

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

λ2eλx−5λeλx−14eλx=0eλx(λ2−5λ−14)=0.

The auxiliary equation is therefore λ2−5λ−14=0.

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

(λ+2)(λ−7)=0,

and so λ=−2 or λ=7.

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is y=Ae−2x+Be7x.

Now let us find constants A and B.

Substituting y(1)=2 into the general solution gives

Ae−2+Be7=2.

We now need to apply the condition y′(1)=5. First, we differentiate y to find y′:

y′=−2Ae−2x+7Be7x

Substituting y′(0)=2 into the above gives

−2Ae−2+7Be7=5.

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for A and B:

{Ae−2+Be7=2−2Ae−2+7Be7=5

Solving this system gives A=e2,B=e−7.

Now we get the solution to the initial value problem: y=e2⋅e−2x+e−7⋅e7xy=e−2x+2+e7x−7

content.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-5\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}-14{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -14) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -14 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
(\lambda +2)(\lambda -7)=0,
$$

and so $\lambda =-2$ or $\lambda =7.$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{7x}.
$$

Now let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
A{e}^{-2}+B{e}^{7}=2.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=5.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-2A{e}^{-2x}+7B{e}^{7x}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the above gives

$$
-2A{e}^{-2}+7B{e}^{7}=5.
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A{e}^{-2}+B{e}^{7}=2 \\ -2A{e}^{-2}+7B{e}^{7}=5\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A={e}^{2},B={e}^{-7}.$

Now we get the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2}\cdot {e}^{-2x}+{e}^{-7}\cdot {e}^{7x} \\ y & ={e}^{-2x+2}+{e}^{7x-7}\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 2
?

Given that the differential equation y″+7y′+10y=0 has the general solution y=Ae−5x+Be−2x, solve the initial value problem y″+7y′+10y=0,y(0)=−3,y′(0)=−3.

a
y=2e−5x−5e−2x
b
y=−e−5x−2e−2x
c
y=e−5x−4e−2x
d
y=3e−5x−6e−2x
e
y=−5e−5x+2e−2x
Submit

decision.explanation: The initial conditions give A+B=-3 and -5A-2B=-3. Substituting B=-3-A yields -3A+6=-3, so A=3 and B=-6. Therefore option d satisfies both initial conditions and the given differential equation.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+7{y}^{′}+10y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=A{e}^{-5x}+B{e}^{-2x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+7{y}^{′}+10y=0,\,y(0)=-3,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-3.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=-3$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B=-3.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-3,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-5A{e}^{-5x}-2B{e}^{-2x}.
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=-3$ into the above to get

$$
-5A-2B=-3.
$$

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=-3 \\ -5A-2B=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=3,B=-6.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=3{e}^{-5x}-6{e}^{-2x}.
$$

Question 2
?

Given that the differential equation y″+7y′+10y=0 has the general solution y=Ae−5x+Be−2x, solve the initial value problem y″+7y′+10y=0,y(0)=−3,y′(0)=−3.

a
y=2e−5x−5e−2x
b
y=−e−5x−2e−2x
c
y=e−5x−4e−2x
d
y=3e−5x−6e−2x
e
y=−5e−5x+2e−2x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We find the constants A and B using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(0)=−3 into the general solution gives A+B=−3.

  • To apply the condition y′(0)=−3, we first differentiate y to get y′=−5Ae−5x−2Be−2x. Then, we substitute y′(0)=−3 into the above to get −5A−2B=−3.

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system: {A+B=−3−5A−2B=−3

Solving this system gives A=3,B=−6.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=3e−5x−6e−2x.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms A=3 and B=-6, giving option d. Directly, y(0)=3-6=-3 and y'(0)=-15+12=-3. Both exponential terms satisfy the differential equation because -5 and -2 are roots of r^2+7r+10=0. Option b is incorrect because its derivative at zero is 9.

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Distinct Real Roots
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+7{y}^{′}+10y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=A{e}^{-5x}+B{e}^{-2x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+7{y}^{′}+10y=0,\,y(0)=-3,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-3.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=-3$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B=-3.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-3,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-5A{e}^{-5x}-2B{e}^{-2x}.
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=-3$ into the above to get

$$
-5A-2B=-3.
$$

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=-3 \\ -5A-2B=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=3,B=-6.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=3{e}^{-5x}-6{e}^{-2x}.
$$

before.html:
Question 3
?

Given that the differential equation y″+7y′+12y=0

has the general solution

y=Ae−3x+Be−4x,

solve the initial value problem

y″+7y′+12y=0,y(0)=−3,y′(0)=2.

a
y=3e−3x−6e−4x
b
y=−10e−3x+7e−4x
c
y=−12e−3x+9e−4x
d
y=7e−3x−10e−4x
e
y=−9e−3x+6e−4x
Submit

decision.explanation: The initial conditions give A+B=-3 and -3A-4B=2. Substituting B=-3-A gives A+12=2, so A=-10 and B=7. Option b therefore has y(0)=-3 and y'(0)=30-28=2, and its exponential terms satisfy the differential equation.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+7{y}^{′}+12y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{-4x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+7{y}^{′}+12y=0,\,y(0)=-3,\,{y}^{′}(0)=2.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=-3$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B=-3.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3x}-4B{e}^{-4x}.
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the above to get

$$
-3A-4B=2.
$$

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=-3 \\ -3A-4B=2\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-10,B=7.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=-10{e}^{-3x}+7{e}^{-4x}.
$$

after.html:
Question 3
?

Given that the differential equation y″+7y′+12y=0

has the general solution

y=Ae−3x+Be−4x,

solve the initial value problem

y″+7y′+12y=0,y(0)=−3,y′(0)=2.

a
y=3e−3x−6e−4x
b
y=−10e−3x+7e−4x
c
y=−12e−3x+9e−4x
d
y=7e−3x−10e−4x
e
y=−9e−3x+6e−4x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We find the constants A and B using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(0)=−3 into the general solution gives A+B=−3.

  • To apply the condition y′(0)=2, we first differentiate y to get y′=−3Ae−3x−4Be−4x. Then, we substitute y′(0)=2 into the above to get −3A−4B=2.

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

{A+B=−3−3A−4B=2

Solving this system gives A=−10,B=7.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=−10e−3x+7e−4x.

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Distinct Real Roots
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+7{y}^{′}+12y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{-4x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+7{y}^{′}+12y=0,\,y(0)=-3,\,{y}^{′}(0)=2.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=-3$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B=-3.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3x}-4B{e}^{-4x}.
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the above to get

$$
-3A-4B=2.
$$

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=-3 \\ -3A-4B=2\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-10,B=7.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=-10{e}^{-3x}+7{e}^{-4x}.
$$

Question 4
?

Given that the differential equation y″−6y′+8y=0

has the general solution

y=Ae2x+Be4x,

solve the initial value problem

y″−6y′+8y=0,y(0)=9,y′(0)=24.

a
y=8e2x+e4x
b
y=e2x+8e4x
c
y=2e2x+7e4x
d
y=5e2x+4e4x
e
y=6e2x+3e4x
Submit

decision.explanation: The initial conditions give A+B=9 and 2A+4B=24. Subtracting twice the first equation from the second gives 2B=6, so B=3 and A=6. Thus option e satisfies the differential equation, y(0)=9, and y'(0)=12+12=24.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-6{y}^{′}+8y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{4x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-6{y}^{′}+8y=0,\,y(0)=9,\,{y}^{′}(0)=24.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=9$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B=9.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=24,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=2A{e}^{2x}+4B{e}^{4x}.
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=24$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}2A+4B & =24 \\ A+2B & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=9 \\ A+2B=12\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=6,B=3.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=6{e}^{2x}+3{e}^{4x}.
$$

Question 4
?

Given that the differential equation y″−6y′+8y=0

has the general solution

y=Ae2x+Be4x,

solve the initial value problem

y″−6y′+8y=0,y(0)=9,y′(0)=24.

a
y=8e2x+e4x
b
y=e2x+8e4x
c
y=2e2x+7e4x
d
y=5e2x+4e4x
e
y=6e2x+3e4x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We find the constants A and B using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(0)=9 into the general solution gives A+B=9.

  • To apply the condition y′(0)=24, we first differentiate y to get y′=2Ae2x+4Be4x. Then, we substitute y′(0)=24 into the above to get 2A+4B=24A+2B=12.

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

{A+B=9A+2B=12

Solving this system gives A=6,B=3.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=6e2x+3e4x.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms A=6 and B=3. Option e gives y(0)=6+3=9 and y'(0)=12+12=24. Its exponential terms satisfy the differential equation since 2 and 4 solve r^2-6r+8=0. Option d instead gives y'(0)=26.

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Distinct Real Roots
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-6{y}^{′}+8y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{4x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-6{y}^{′}+8y=0,\,y(0)=9,\,{y}^{′}(0)=24.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=9$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B=9.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=24,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=2A{e}^{2x}+4B{e}^{4x}.
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=24$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}2A+4B & =24 \\ A+2B & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=9 \\ A+2B=12\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=6,B=3.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=6{e}^{2x}+3{e}^{4x}.
$$

Question 5
?

Solve the initial value problem y″−8y′+15y=0,y(0)=2,y′(0)=2.

a
y=−4e3x+6e5x
b
y=−2e3x+4e5x
c
y=4e3x−2e5x
d
y=e3x+e5x
e
y=3e3x−e5x
Submit

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation factors as (r-3)(r-5)=0, so y=Ae^{3x}+Be^{5x}. The initial conditions give A+B=2 and 3A+5B=2. Thus B=-2 and A=4, yielding option c. Directly, y(0)=4-2=2 and y'(0)=12-10=2.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +15 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -5) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{3x}+B{e}^{5x}.
$$

Now we find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B=2.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=3A{e}^{3x}+5B{e}^{5x}.
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the above to get

$$
3A+5B=2.
$$

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=2 \\ 3A+5B=2\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=4,B=-2.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$

after.html:
Question 5
?

Solve the initial value problem y″−8y′+15y=0,y(0)=2,y′(0)=2.

a
y=−4e3x+6e5x
b
y=−2e3x+4e5x
c
y=4e3x−2e5x
d
y=e3x+e5x
e
y=3e3x−e5x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

λ2−8λ+15=0(λ−3)(λ−5)=0λ=3,5

So, the general solution to the differential equation is y=Ae3x+Be5x.

Now we find the constants A and B using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(0)=2 into the general solution gives A+B=2.

  • To apply the condition y′(0)=2, we first differentiate y to get y′=3Ae3x+5Be5x. Then, we substitute y′(0)=2 into the above to get 3A+5B=2.

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

{A+B=23A+5B=2

Solving this system gives A=4,B=−2.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=4e3x−2e5x.

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Distinct Real Roots
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +15 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -5) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{3x}+B{e}^{5x}.
$$

Now we find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B=2.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=3A{e}^{3x}+5B{e}^{5x}.
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the above to get

$$
3A+5B=2.
$$

Putting the two equations from above together, we have the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=2 \\ 3A+5B=2\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=4,B=-2.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4{e}^{3x}-2{e}^{5x}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+16y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=A{e}^{-4x}+Bx{e}^{-4x},

solve the initial value problem

before.html:
Question 6
?

Given that the differential equation y″+8y′+16y=0

has the general solution y=Ae−4x+Bxe−4x,

solve the initial value problem y″+8y′+16y=0,y(0)=1,y′(0)=−2.

a
y=e−4x+xe−4x
b
y=e−4x−xe−4x
c
y=e−4x−2xe−4x
d
y=e−4x−3xe−4x
e
y=e−4x+2xe−4x
Submit

decision.explanation: From y(0)=1, we get A=1. Differentiating gives y'=(-4A+B-4Bx)e^{-4x}, so y'(0)=-4A+B=-2 implies B=2. Thus option e satisfies the initial conditions and the given differential equation.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+16y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=A{e}^{-4x}+Bx{e}^{-4x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,y(0)=1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-2.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
A=1.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-4A{e}^{-4x}+B{e}^{-4x}-4Bx{e}^{-4x}.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=-2$ into the above gives

$$
-4A+B=-2.
$$

Using the fact that $A=1$ gives $B=2.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{-4x}+2x{e}^{-4x}.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Repeated Roots
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+16y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=A{e}^{-4x}+Bx{e}^{-4x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,y(0)=1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-2.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
A=1.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-4A{e}^{-4x}+B{e}^{-4x}-4Bx{e}^{-4x}.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=-2$ into the above gives

$$
-4A+B=-2.
$$

Using the fact that $A=1$ gives $B=2.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{-4x}+2x{e}^{-4x}.
$$

Question 7

Given that the functions y1(x)=e4x and y2(x)=xe4x are solutions to the equation y″−8y′+16y=0, solve the following initial value problem.

y″−8y′+16y=0,y(0)=1,y′(0)=−1.

a
y=e4x+2xe4x
b
y=e4x+4xe4x
c
y=e4x−5xe4x
d
y=e4x−6xe4x
e
y=e4x−xe4x
Submit

decision.explanation: Write y=(A+Bx)e^{4x}. The condition y(0)=1 gives A=1. Since y'(0)=4A+B=-1, B=-5. Thus option c satisfies both initial conditions and, as a linear combination of the given solutions, the differential equation.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Given that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4x}$ are solutions to the equation ${y}^{″}-8{y}^{′}+16y=0,$ solve the following initial value problem.

$$
{y}^{″}-8{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,y(0)=1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-1.
$$
after.worked_solution:
According to the superposition principle, any linear combination of the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$  and ${y}_{2}(x)$  must be a solution to the original differential equation.

Hence, the general solution is: 

$$
y={c}_{1}{e}^{4x}+{c}_{2}x{e}^{4x}
$$

Now, we find constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
{c}_{1}=1.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$ 

$$
{y}^{′}=(4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}){e}^{4x}+4{c}_{2}x{e}^{4x}
$$

Substituting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=-1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1=4(1)+{c}_{2}\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{4x}-5x{e}^{4x}.
$$

after.html:
Question 7
?

Given that the functions y1(x)=e4x and y2(x)=xe4x are solutions to the equation y″−8y′+16y=0, solve the following initial value problem.

y″−8y′+16y=0,y(0)=1,y′(0)=−1.

a
y=e4x+2xe4x
b
y=e4x+4xe4x
c
y=e4x−5xe4x
d
y=e4x−6xe4x
e
y=e4x−xe4x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

According to the superposition principle, any linear combination of the functions y1(x) and y2(x) must be a solution to the original differential equation.

Hence, the general solution is: y=c1e4x+c2xe4x

Now, we find constants c1 and c2.

Substituting y(0)=1 into the general solution gives

c1=1.

We now need to apply the condition y′(0)=−1. First, we differentiate y to find y′:

y′=(4c1+c2)e4x+4c2xe4x

Substituting c1=1 and y′(0)=−1 into the above gives

−1=4(1)+c2⟹c2=−5.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

y=e4x−5xe4x.

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Repeated Roots
content.problem:
Given that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4x}$ are solutions to the equation ${y}^{″}-8{y}^{′}+16y=0,$ solve the following initial value problem.

$$
{y}^{″}-8{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,y(0)=1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-1.
$$
content.worked_solution:
According to the superposition principle, any linear combination of the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$  and ${y}_{2}(x)$  must be a solution to the original differential equation.

Hence, the general solution is: 

$$
y={c}_{1}{e}^{4x}+{c}_{2}x{e}^{4x}
$$

Now, we find constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
{c}_{1}=1.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$ 

$$
{y}^{′}=(4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}){e}^{4x}+4{c}_{2}x{e}^{4x}
$$

Substituting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=-1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1=4(1)+{c}_{2}\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{4x}-5x{e}^{4x}.
$$

Solve the initial value problem y″−8y′+16y=0,y(1)=2,  y′(1)=−1.

a
y=11e4x−4−9xe4x−4
b
y=5e4x−4−3xe4x−4
c
y=−7e4x−4+9xe4x−4
d
y=3e2x−2−xe2x−2
e
y=8e2x−2−6xe2x−2
Submit

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation is (r-4)^2=0, so write y=(A+Bx)e^{4x-4}. The initial conditions give A+B=2 and 4(A+B)+B=-1. Hence B=-9 and A=11, yielding option a. It satisfies y(1)=2 and y'(1)=8-9=-1.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-8\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+16{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -4)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =4$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{4x}+Bx{e}^{4x}.
$$

Let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
A{e}^{4}+B{e}^{4}=2.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=4A{e}^{4x}+B{e}^{4x}+4Bx{e}^{4x}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ into the above gives

$$
4A{e}^{4}+5B{e}^{4}=-1.
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A{e}^{4}+B{e}^{4}=2 \\ 4A{e}^{4}+5B{e}^{4}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=11{e}^{-4},B=-9{e}^{-4}.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =11{e}^{-4}\cdot {e}^{4x}-9{e}^{-4}\cdot x{e}^{4x} \\  & =11{e}^{4x-4}-9x{e}^{4x-4}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Repeated Roots
content.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-8\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+16{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -4)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =4$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{4x}+Bx{e}^{4x}.
$$

Let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
A{e}^{4}+B{e}^{4}=2.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=4A{e}^{4x}+B{e}^{4x}+4Bx{e}^{4x}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ into the above gives

$$
4A{e}^{4}+5B{e}^{4}=-1.
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A{e}^{4}+B{e}^{4}=2 \\ 4A{e}^{4}+5B{e}^{4}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=11{e}^{-4},B=-9{e}^{-4}.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =11{e}^{-4}\cdot {e}^{4x}-9{e}^{-4}\cdot x{e}^{4x} \\  & =11{e}^{4x-4}-9x{e}^{4x-4}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation is (r+10)^2=0, so y=(A+Bx)e^{-10x}. From y(0)=5, A=5. Then y'(0)=B-10A=-5 gives B=45. Therefore option b satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+20\lambda +100 & =0 \\ {(\lambda +10)}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We have a repeated root $\lambda =-10,$ so we have the following general solution:

$$
y=A{e}^{-10x}+Bx{e}^{-10x}
$$

We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=5$ into the general solution gives

$$
A=5.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-5,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-10A{e}^{-10x}+B{e}^{-10x}-10Bx{e}^{-10x}.
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=-5$ into the above to get

$$
-10A+B=-5.
$$

Using the fact that $A=5$ gives $B=45.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=5{e}^{-10x}+45x{e}^{-10x}.

Question 9
?

Solve the initial value problem y″+20y′+100y=0,y(0)=5,y′(0)=−5.

a
y=−5e10x+xe10x
b
y=5e−10x+45xe−10x
c
 y=5e−10x+27xe−10x
d
y=5e−10x+xe−10x
e
y=5e10x+2e−10x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

λ2+20λ+100=0(λ+10)2=0

We have a repeated root λ=−10, so we have the following general solution:

y=Ae−10x+Bxe−10x

We find the constants A and B using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(0)=5 into the general solution gives A=5.

  • To apply the condition y′(0)=−5, we first differentiate y to get y′=−10Ae−10x+Be−10x−10Bxe−10x. Then, we substitute y′(0)=−5 into the above to get −10A+B=−5. Using the fact that A=5 gives B=45.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=5e−10x+45xe−10x.

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Repeated Roots
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+20\lambda +100 & =0 \\ {(\lambda +10)}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We have a repeated root $\lambda =-10,$ so we have the following general solution:

$$
y=A{e}^{-10x}+Bx{e}^{-10x}
$$

We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=5$ into the general solution gives

$$
A=5.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-5,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-10A{e}^{-10x}+B{e}^{-10x}-10Bx{e}^{-10x}.
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=-5$ into the above to get

$$
-10A+B=-5.
$$

Using the fact that $A=5$ gives $B=45.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=5{e}^{-10x}+45x{e}^{-10x}.
$$

Question 10
?

Solve the initial value problem y″+3y′+9y4=0,y(1)=e−1/2,  y′(1)=12e−1/2.

a
y=xe−3x/2+1
b
y=−2ex/2−1+3xex/2−1
c
y=−e−3x/2+1+2xe−3x/2+1
d
y=3e−3x/2+1−2xe−3x/2+1
e
y=−ex/2−1+2xex/2−1
Submit

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation is (r+3/2)^2=0, so write y=(A+Bx)e^{-3x/2+1}. The initial conditions give A+B=1 and B-(3/2)(A+B)=1/2. Thus B=2 and A=-1, which is option c and satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+3\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{9}{4}{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +\frac{9}{4}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +\frac{9}{4} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +\frac{3}{2})(\lambda +\frac{3}{2}) & =0 \\ {(\lambda +\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =\frac{3}{2}$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{-3x/2}+Bx{e}^{-3x/2}.
$$

Let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 
Substituting $y(1)={e}^{-1/2}$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{-3/2}+B{e}^{-3/2} & ={e}^{-1/2} \\ A+B & =e.\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-1/2}.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-\frac{3}{2}A{e}^{-3/2x}+B{e}^{-3/2x}-\frac{3}{2}Bx{e}^{-3/2x}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-1/2}$ into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}A{e}^{-3/2}-\frac{1}{2}B{e}^{-3/2} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-1/2} \\ -\frac{3}{2}A-\frac{1}{2}B & =\frac{1}{2}e \\ -3A-B & =e\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=e \\ -3A-B=e\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-e,B=2e.$

Now we get the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-e\cdot {e}^{-3x/2}+2e\cdot x{e}^{-3x/2} \\  & =-{e}^{-3x/2+1}+2x{e}^{-3x/2+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Solve the initial value problem y″+3y′+9y4=0,y(1)=e−1/2,  y′(1)=12e−1/2.

a
y=xe−3x/2+1
b
y=−2ex/2−1+3xex/2−1
c
y=−e−3x/2+1+2xe−3x/2+1
d
y=3e−3x/2+1−2xe−3x/2+1
e
y=−ex/2−1+2xex/2−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let y=eλx. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λeλx,y″=λ2eλx.

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives:

λ2eλx+3λeλx+94eλx=0eλx(λ2+3λ+94)=0

The auxiliary equation is therefore λ2+3λ+94=0.

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives (λ+32)(λ+32)=0(λ+32)2=0.

Therefore, λ=32 is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is y=Ae−3x/2+Bxe−3x/2. Let us find constants A and B. Substituting y(1)=e−1/2 into the general solution gives

Ae−3/2+Be−3/2=e−1/2A+B=e.

We now need to apply the condition y′(1)=12e−1/2. First, we differentiate y to find y′: y′=−32Ae−3/2x+Be−3/2x−32Bxe−3/2x Substituting y′(1)=12e−1/2 into the above gives:

−32Ae−3/2−12Be−3/2=12e−1/2−32A−12B=12e−3A−B=e

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for A and B:

{A+B=e−3A−B=e

Solving this system gives A=−e,B=2e.

Now we get the solution to the initial value problem: y=−e⋅e−3x/2+2e⋅xe−3x/2=−e−3x/2+1+2xe−3x/2+1

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Repeated Roots
content.worked_solution:
Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+3\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{9}{4}{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +\frac{9}{4}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +\frac{9}{4} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +\frac{3}{2})(\lambda +\frac{3}{2}) & =0 \\ {(\lambda +\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =\frac{3}{2}$ is a repeated root.

So the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{-3x/2}+Bx{e}^{-3x/2}.
$$

Let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 
Substituting $y(1)={e}^{-1/2}$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{-3/2}+B{e}^{-3/2} & ={e}^{-1/2} \\ A+B & =e.\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-1/2}.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-\frac{3}{2}A{e}^{-3/2x}+B{e}^{-3/2x}-\frac{3}{2}Bx{e}^{-3/2x}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-1/2}$ into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}A{e}^{-3/2}-\frac{1}{2}B{e}^{-3/2} & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-1/2} \\ -\frac{3}{2}A-\frac{1}{2}B & =\frac{1}{2}e \\ -3A-B & =e\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
{\begin{aligned}A+B=e \\ -3A-B=e\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-e,B=2e.$

Now we get the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-e\cdot {e}^{-3x/2}+2e\cdot x{e}^{-3x/2} \\  & =-{e}^{-3x/2+1}+2x{e}^{-3x/2+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Solve the initial value problem y″+64y=0,y(π)=1,y′(π)=4.

a
y=cos⁡8x+2sin⁡8x
b
y=cos⁡8x−12sin⁡8x
c
y=cos⁡8x+sin⁡8x
d
y=cos⁡8x+12sin⁡8x
e
y=cos⁡8x−2sin⁡8x
Submit

decision.explanation: The general solution is y=A cos(8x)+B sin(8x). Since cos(8π)=1 and sin(8π)=0, y(π)=1 gives A=1. Differentiating gives y'(π)=8B=4, so B=1/2. Thus option d satisfies the equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-64 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 8\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =P\operatorname{cos}⁡8x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡8x\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(\pi )=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}P=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=4,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-8P\operatorname{sin}⁡8x+8Q\operatorname{cos}⁡8x.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(\pi )=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}8Q=4\,⟹\,Q=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=\operatorname{cos}⁡8x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡8x.
$$

Question 11
?

Solve the initial value problem y″+64y=0,y(π)=1,y′(π)=4.

a
y=cos⁡8x+2sin⁡8x
b
y=cos⁡8x−12sin⁡8x
c
y=cos⁡8x+sin⁡8x
d
y=cos⁡8x+12sin⁡8x
e
y=cos⁡8x−2sin⁡8x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

λ2+64=0λ2=−64λ=±8i.

So, we have the following general solution:

y=Pcos⁡8x+Qsin⁡8x

We find the constants P and Q using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(π)=1 into the general solution gives P=1.

  • To apply the condition y′(π)=4, we first differentiate y to get y′=−8Psin⁡8x+8Qcos⁡8x. Substituting y′(π)=4 into the above gives 8Q=4⟹Q=12.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

y=cos⁡8x+12sin⁡8x.

$$
y=\operatorname{cos}⁡8x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡8x.

Question 12
?

Solve the initial value problem y″+49y=0,y(π)=−2,y′(π)=7.

a
 y=2cos⁡7x−2sin⁡7x
b
y=2cos⁡7x−sin⁡7x
c
 y=2cos⁡7x+2sin⁡7x
d
 y=2cos⁡7x−7sin⁡7x
e
y=2cos⁡7x+sin⁡7x
Submit

decision.explanation: The general solution is y=A cos(7x)+B sin(7x). Since cos(7π)=-1 and sin(7π)=0, y(π)=-A=-2 gives A=2. Also y'(π)=-7B=7 gives B=-1. Thus option b satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 12
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-49 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 7\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =P\operatorname{cos}⁡7x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡7x\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(\pi )=-2$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-P=-2\,⟹\,P=2.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=7,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-7P\operatorname{sin}⁡7x+7Q\operatorname{cos}⁡7x.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(\pi )=7$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-7Q=7\,⟹\,Q=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡7x-\operatorname{sin}⁡7x.
$$

Question 12
?

Solve the initial value problem y″+49y=0,y(π)=−2,y′(π)=7.

a
 y=2cos⁡7x−2sin⁡7x
b
y=2cos⁡7x−sin⁡7x
c
 y=2cos⁡7x+2sin⁡7x
d
 y=2cos⁡7x−7sin⁡7x
e
y=2cos⁡7x+sin⁡7x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

λ2+49=0λ2=−49λ=±7i.

So, we have the following general solution:

y=Pcos⁡7x+Qsin⁡7x

We find the constants P and Q using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(π)=−2 into the general solution gives −P=−2⟹P=2.

  • To apply the condition y′(π)=7, we first differentiate y to get y′=−7Psin⁡7x+7Qcos⁡7x. Substituting y′(π)=7 into the above gives −7Q=7⟹Q=−1.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

y=2cos⁡7x−sin⁡7x.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option b. Its derivative is y'=-14 sin(7x)-7 cos(7x), giving y(π)=-2 and y'(π)=7. Also y''=-49y, so the differential equation holds. Option d instead gives y'(π)=49.

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Imaginary Roots
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-49 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 7\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =P\operatorname{cos}⁡7x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡7x\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(\pi )=-2$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-P=-2\,⟹\,P=2.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=7,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-7P\operatorname{sin}⁡7x+7Q\operatorname{cos}⁡7x.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(\pi )=7$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-7Q=7\,⟹\,Q=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡7x-\operatorname{sin}⁡7x.
$$

λ2+100=0λ2=−100λ=±10i.

y=Pcos⁡10x+Qsin⁡10x

Question 14
?

Solve the initial value problem y″+144y=0,y(π8)=1,y′(π8)=24.

a
y=2cos⁡x−sin⁡12x
b
y=cos⁡12x−sin⁡12x
c
y=−cos⁡12x−sin⁡12x
d
y=−sin⁡12x
e
y=2cos⁡12x−sin⁡12x
Submit

decision.explanation: Write y=A cos(12x)+B sin(12x). At x=π/8, cos(3π/2)=0 and sin(3π/2)=-1, so -B=1 and B=-1. The derivative condition gives 12A=24, hence A=2. Option e satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+144 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-144 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 12\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =P\operatorname{cos}⁡12x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡12x\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(\frac{\pi }{8})=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-Q=1\,⟹\,Q=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8})=24,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-12P\operatorname{sin}⁡12x+12Q\operatorname{cos}⁡12x.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8})=24$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}12P=24\,⟹\,P=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡12x-\operatorname{sin}⁡12x.
$$

a

b
y=−4cos⁡(2x)+42sin⁡(2x)

decision.explanation: The general solution is y=A cos(√2 x)+B sin(√2 x). The condition y(0)=-4 gives A=-4, and y'(0)=√2 B=4√2 gives B=4. Thus option a satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =P\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=-4$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}P=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=4\sqrt{2},$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-\sqrt{2}P\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+\sqrt{2}Q\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=4\sqrt{2}$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2}Q=4\sqrt{2}\,⟹\,Q=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Question 15
?

Solve the initial value problem y″+2y=0,y(0)=−4,y′(0)=42.

a
y=−4cos⁡(2x)+4sin⁡(2x)
b
y=−4cos⁡(2x)+42sin⁡(2x)
c
y=−4cos⁡(2x)+2sin⁡(2x)
d
y=−4cos⁡(2x)−42sin⁡(2x)
e
y=−4cos⁡(2x)−2sin⁡(2x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

λ2+2=0λ2=−2λ=±2i.

So, we have the following general solution:

y=Pcos⁡(2x)+Qsin⁡(2x)

We find the constants P and Q using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(0)=−4 into the general solution gives P=−4.

  • To apply the condition y′(0)=42, we first differentiate y to get y′=−2Psin⁡(2x)+2Qcos⁡(2x). Substituting y′(0)=42 into the above gives 2Q=42⟹Q=4.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

y=−4cos⁡(2x)+4sin⁡(2x).

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Imaginary Roots
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =P\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(0)=-4$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}P=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=4\sqrt{2},$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-\sqrt{2}P\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+\sqrt{2}Q\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=4\sqrt{2}$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2}Q=4\sqrt{2}\,⟹\,Q=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Question 16
?

Solve the initial value problem y″−4y′+8y=0,y(π2)=eπ,  y′(π2)=4eπ.

a
y=e2x(3sin⁡2x−cos⁡2x)
b
y=e2x(cos⁡x+sin⁡x)
c
y=−e2x(cos⁡2x+sin⁡2x)
d
y=−e2x(2cos⁡x−sin⁡x)
e
y=−e2x(cos⁡2x+2sin⁡2x)
Submit

decision.explanation: The characteristic roots are 2±2i, giving y=e^{2x}(A cos(2x)+B sin(2x)). At x=π/2, the value condition gives -A=1, so A=-1. The derivative condition gives -2A-2B=4, hence B=-1. Therefore option c satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 16
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(\frac{\pi }{2})={e}^{\pi }$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-P{e}^{\pi } & ={e}^{\pi } \\ P & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=4{e}^{\pi },$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=2{e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+{e}^{2x}(-2P\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2Q\operatorname{cos}⁡2x).
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=4{e}^{\pi }$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2P{e}^{\pi }-2Q{e}^{\pi } & =4{e}^{\pi } \\ -2P-2Q & =4 \\ 2-2Q & =4 \\ Q & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $P=-1$ and $Q=-1.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =-{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 16
?

Solve the initial value problem y″−4y′+8y=0,y(π2)=eπ,  y′(π2)=4eπ.

a
y=e2x(3sin⁡2x−cos⁡2x)
b
y=e2x(cos⁡x+sin⁡x)
c
y=−e2x(cos⁡2x+sin⁡2x)
d
y=−e2x(2cos⁡x−sin⁡x)
e
y=−e2x(cos⁡2x+2sin⁡2x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial by completing the square:

λ2−4λ+8=0(λ2−4λ+4)−4+8=0(λ−2)2+4=0(λ−2)2=−4λ−2=±2iλ=2±2i.

So, we have the following general solution:

y=e2x(Pcos⁡2x+Qsin⁡2x)

We find the constants P and Q using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(π2)=eπ into the general solution gives −Peπ=eπP=−1.

  • To apply the condition y′(π2)=4eπ, we first differentiate y to get y′=2e2x(Pcos⁡2x+Qsin⁡2x)+e2x(−2Psin⁡2x+2Qcos⁡2x). Substituting y′(π2)=4eπ into the above gives −2Peπ−2Qeπ=4eπ−2P−2Q=42−2Q=4Q=−1.

So we have P=−1 and Q=−1.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=e2x(−cos⁡2x−sin⁡2x)=−e2x(cos⁡2x+sin⁡2x).

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(\frac{\pi }{2})={e}^{\pi }$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-P{e}^{\pi } & ={e}^{\pi } \\ P & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=4{e}^{\pi },$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=2{e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+{e}^{2x}(-2P\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2Q\operatorname{cos}⁡2x).
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=4{e}^{\pi }$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2P{e}^{\pi }-2Q{e}^{\pi } & =4{e}^{\pi } \\ -2P-2Q & =4 \\ 2-2Q & =4 \\ Q & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $P=-1$ and $Q=-1.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =-{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 17
?

Given that the differential equation y″−2y′+26y=0

has the general solution y=ex(Pcos⁡5x+Qsin⁡5x),

solve the initial value problem y″−2y′+26y=0,y(0)=−4,y′(0)=1.

a
y=ex(−4cos⁡5x−5sin⁡5x)
b
y=ex(−4cos⁡5x+4sin⁡5x)
c
y=ex(−4cos⁡5x−4sin⁡5x)
d
y=ex(−4cos⁡5x−sin⁡5x)
e
y=ex(−4cos⁡5x+sin⁡5x)
Submit

decision.explanation: The condition y(0)=-4 gives P=-4. Differentiating the general solution gives y'(0)=P+5Q=1, so -4+5Q=1 and Q=1. Thus option e satisfies both initial conditions and the differential equation.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+26y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={e}^{x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡5x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡5x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+26y=0,\,y(0)=-4,\,{y}^{′}(0)=1.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=-4$ into the general solution gives

$$
P=-4.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=1,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}={e}^{x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡5x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡5x)+{e}^{x}(-5P\operatorname{sin}⁡5x+5Q\operatorname{cos}⁡5x).
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=1$ into the above to get

$$
P+5Q=1.
$$

Using the fact that $P=-4$ gives $Q=1.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{x}(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡5x+\operatorname{sin}⁡5x).
$$

after.html:
Question 17
?

Given that the differential equation y″−2y′+26y=0

has the general solution y=ex(Pcos⁡5x+Qsin⁡5x),

solve the initial value problem y″−2y′+26y=0,y(0)=−4,y′(0)=1.

a
y=ex(−4cos⁡5x−5sin⁡5x)
b
y=ex(−4cos⁡5x+4sin⁡5x)
c
y=ex(−4cos⁡5x−4sin⁡5x)
d
y=ex(−4cos⁡5x−sin⁡5x)
e
y=ex(−4cos⁡5x+sin⁡5x)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We find the constants P and Q using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(0)=−4 into the general solution gives P=−4.

  • To apply the condition y′(0)=1, we first differentiate y to get y′=ex(Pcos⁡5x+Qsin⁡5x)+ex(−5Psin⁡5x+5Qcos⁡5x). Then, we substitute y′(0)=1 into the above to get P+5Q=1. Using the fact that P=−4 gives Q=1.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=ex(−4cos⁡5x+sin⁡5x).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms P=-4 and Q=1, giving option e. Its derivative is e^x(cos(5x)+21 sin(5x)), so y(0)=-4 and y'(0)=1. The characteristic roots 1±5i ensure it satisfies the differential equation. Option b instead gives y'(0)=-4+20=16.

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+26y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={e}^{x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡5x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡5x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+26y=0,\,y(0)=-4,\,{y}^{′}(0)=1.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=-4$ into the general solution gives

$$
P=-4.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=1,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}={e}^{x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡5x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡5x)+{e}^{x}(-5P\operatorname{sin}⁡5x+5Q\operatorname{cos}⁡5x).
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=1$ into the above to get

$$
P+5Q=1.
$$

Using the fact that $P=-4$ gives $Q=1.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{x}(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡5x+\operatorname{sin}⁡5x).
$$

a

b

c

decision.explanation: The condition y(0)=2 gives P=2. Differentiating the general solution gives y'(0)=4P+7Q=1, so 8+7Q=1 and Q=-1. Thus option e satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 18
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}-8{y}^{′}+65y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={e}^{4x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡7x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡7x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-8{y}^{′}+65y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=1.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
P=2.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=1,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=4{e}^{4x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡7x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡7x)+{e}^{4x}(-7P\operatorname{sin}⁡7x+7Q\operatorname{cos}⁡7x).
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=1$ into the above to get

$$
4P+7Q=1.
$$

Using the fact that $P=2$ gives $Q=-1.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{4x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡7x-\operatorname{sin}⁡7x).
$$

  • To apply the condition y′(0)=1, we first differentiate y to get y′=4e4x(Pcos⁡7x+Qsin⁡7x)+e4x(−7Psin⁡7x+7Qcos⁡7x). Then, we substitute y′(0)=1 into the above to get 4P+7Q=1. Using the fact that P=2 gives Q=−1.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=e4x(2cos⁡7x−sin⁡7x).

Question 19

Given that the differential equation y″+6y′+13y=0 has the general solution y=e−3x(Pcos⁡2x+Qsin⁡2x), solve the initial value problem y″+6y′+13y=0,y(0)=2,y′(0)=−4.

a
y=e−3x(2cos⁡2x+2sin⁡2x)
b
y=e−3x(2cos⁡2x+3sin⁡2x)
c
y=e−3x(2cos⁡2x−2sin⁡2x)
d
y=e−3x(2cos⁡2x+sin⁡2x)
e
y=e−3x(2cos⁡2x−sin⁡2x)
Submit

decision.explanation: The condition y(0)=2 gives P=2. Differentiating gives y'(0)=-3P+2Q=-4, so -6+2Q=-4 and Q=1. Thus option d satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+6{y}^{′}+13y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={e}^{-3x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+6{y}^{′}+13y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-4.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
P=2.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-4,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-3{e}^{-3x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+{e}^{-3x}(-2P\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2Q\operatorname{cos}⁡2x).
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=-4$ into the above to get

$$
-3P+2Q=-4.
$$

Using the fact that $P=2$ gives $Q=1.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{-3x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).
$$

after.html:
Question 19
?

Given that the differential equation y″+6y′+13y=0 has the general solution y=e−3x(Pcos⁡2x+Qsin⁡2x), solve the initial value problem y″+6y′+13y=0,y(0)=2,y′(0)=−4.

a
y=e−3x(2cos⁡2x+2sin⁡2x)
b
y=e−3x(2cos⁡2x+3sin⁡2x)
c
y=e−3x(2cos⁡2x−2sin⁡2x)
d
y=e−3x(2cos⁡2x+sin⁡2x)
e
y=e−3x(2cos⁡2x−sin⁡2x)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We find the constants P and Q using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(0)=2 into the general solution gives P=2.

  • To apply the condition y′(0)=−4, we first differentiate y to get y′=−3e−3x(Pcos⁡2x+Qsin⁡2x)+e−3x(−2Psin⁡2x+2Qcos⁡2x). Then, we substitute y′(0)=−4 into the above to get −3P+2Q=−4. Using the fact that P=2 gives Q=1.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=e−3x(2cos⁡2x+sin⁡2x).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms P=2 and Q=1, giving option d. Its derivative is e^{-3x}(-4 cos(2x)-7 sin(2x)), so y(0)=2 and y'(0)=-4. The characteristic roots -3±2i ensure it satisfies the differential equation. Option a instead gives y'(0)=-2.

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+6{y}^{′}+13y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={e}^{-3x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+6{y}^{′}+13y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-4.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions. 

- Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
P=2.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-4,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-3{e}^{-3x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+{e}^{-3x}(-2P\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2Q\operatorname{cos}⁡2x).
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(0)=-4$ into the above to get

$$
-3P+2Q=-4.
$$

Using the fact that $P=2$ gives $Q=1.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{-3x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).
$$

Question 20
?

Solve the initial value problem y″+4y′+5y=0,y(π2)=e−π,y′(π2)=6e−π.

a
 y=e−2x(−4cos⁡x+sin⁡x)
b
y=e−2x(−8cos⁡x+sin⁡x)
c
 y=−e−2x(4cos⁡x−sin⁡x)
d
 y=e−2x(8cos⁡x+sin⁡x)
e
 y=−2e−2x(6cos⁡x+sin⁡x)
Submit

decision.explanation: The characteristic roots are -2±i, so y=e^{-2x}(A cos(x)+B sin(x)). At x=π/2, the value condition gives B=1. The derivative condition gives -2B-A=6, hence A=-8. Thus option b satisfies the equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 20
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +5 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4)-4+5 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(\frac{\pi }{2})={e}^{-\pi }$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}Q{e}^{-\pi } & ={e}^{-\pi } \\ Q & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=6{e}^{-\pi },$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-2{e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{e}^{-2x}(-P\operatorname{sin}⁡x+Q\operatorname{cos}⁡x).
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=6{e}^{-\pi }$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2Q{e}^{-\pi }-P{e}^{-\pi } & =6{e}^{-\pi } \\ -2Q-P & =6 \\ -2-P & =6 \\ P & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $P=-8$ and $Q=1.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-2x}(-8\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20

Solve the initial value problem y″+4y′+5y=0,y(π2)=e−π,y′(π2)=6e−π.

a
 y=e−2x(−4cos⁡x+sin⁡x)
b
y=e−2x(−8cos⁡x+sin⁡x)
c
 y=−e−2x(4cos⁡x−sin⁡x)
d
 y=e−2x(8cos⁡x+sin⁡x)
e
 y=−2e−2x(6cos⁡x+sin⁡x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial by completing the square:

λ2+4λ+5=0(λ2+4λ+4)−4+5=0(λ+2)2+1=0(λ+2)2=−1λ+2=±iλ=−2±i

So, we have the following general solution:

y=e−2x(Pcos⁡x+Qsin⁡x)

We find the constants P and Q using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(π2)=e−π into the general solution gives Qe−π=e−πQ=1.

  • To apply the condition y′(π2)=6e−π, we first differentiate y to get y′=−2e−2x(Pcos⁡x+Qsin⁡x)+e−2x(−Psin⁡x+Qcos⁡x). Substituting y′(π2)=6e−π into the above gives −2Qe−π−Pe−π=6e−π−2Q−P=6−2−P=6P=−8.

So we have P=−8 and Q=1.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=e−2x(−8cos⁡x+sin⁡x).

content.knowledge_point: Solving Second-Order IVPs When the Characteristic Equation Has Complex Roots
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the roots of the characteristic polynomial by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +5 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4)-4+5 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants $P$ and $Q$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(\frac{\pi }{2})={e}^{-\pi }$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}Q{e}^{-\pi } & ={e}^{-\pi } \\ Q & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=6{e}^{-\pi },$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
{y}^{′}=-2{e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{e}^{-2x}(-P\operatorname{sin}⁡x+Q\operatorname{cos}⁡x).
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=6{e}^{-\pi }$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2Q{e}^{-\pi }-P{e}^{-\pi } & =6{e}^{-\pi } \\ -2Q-P & =6 \\ -2-P & =6 \\ P & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $P=-8$ and $Q=1.$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{-2x}(-8\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$
